lesson.title: The Trade You Can't Avoid: Gain-Bandwidth Product
lesson.summary: Every op-amp carries a fixed product of closed-loop gain and usable bandwidth, meaning a single amplifier can be configured for high gain or wide bandwidth, but not unlimited amounts of both at once.
lesson.body:
Recall closed-loop gain, set by the external feedback network, and op-amp bandwidth, the frequency range over which that gain stays roughly flat before rolling off. That rolloff exists because every op-amp includes an internal compensation capacitor that makes its open-loop gain fall steadily with frequency once past a fairly low corner.

For a large majority of general-purpose op-amps, that open-loop rolloff behaves as a single dominant pole, meaning gain falls at a constant rate on a log-log plot once past that corner frequency. Within the range where the feedback network's demanded closed-loop gain sits comfortably below the op-amp's remaining open-loop gain, the closed-loop bandwidth you actually get is set by where the requested gain line crosses that falling open-loop curve. Because the open-loop curve falls at a constant rate, the closed-loop gain times the closed-loop bandwidth comes out to very nearly a constant for a given chip. That constant is the gain-bandwidth product, listed directly on the datasheet, and it is numerically equal to the frequency at which the open-loop gain would fall to 1, the unity-gain frequency.

The relationship is GBP = Acl times BW, so BW = GBP / Acl.

Take an op-amp with GBP = 1MHz, a reasonably typical figure for a general-purpose part, in the same ballpark as classic parts like the 741. Configure it for a closed-loop gain of 100: BW = 1,000,000 / 100 = 10,000Hz, or 10kHz. Reduce the gain to 10 instead: BW = 1,000,000 / 10 = 100,000Hz, or 100kHz. Same chip, ten times the gain, one tenth the bandwidth. Gain and bandwidth trade directly against each other.

This applies immediately to the instrumentation amplifier example from earlier: with that same 1MHz-GBP op-amp used at a gain of 11, bandwidth = 1,000,000 / 11, approximately 90,900Hz, or about 90.9kHz. That is comfortably wide for most sensor signals, but it is something a designer has to check explicitly rather than assume, especially once gain climbs into the hundreds or thousands, as it often does for weak sensor signals.
